newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma accuses U.S. of provocation as unrest slows.
newsitem.headline: Burma accuses U.S. of provocation as unrest slows.

text.p: Burma and the United States tangled on Friday when Rangoon prevented a U.S. diplomat from meeting opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi and accused Washington of interfering in Burma's internal affairs.

Rangoon also came under fresh international fire, with Europe expressing concern about reports of police brutality in dispersing student protests and the U.N. General Assembly rebuking military leaders for suppressing opposition.

A Burmese government spokesman accused the United States of provocation after Rangoon officials stopped U.S. charge d'affaires Kent Wiedemann from meeting Nobel laureate Suu Kyi, who has been virtually confined to her home since last week's student unrest.

"This is provocative. They should not interfere in our internal affairs," a government spokesman told Reuters. "No other embassies do this. If they want to invite her to lunch, they should do it later when the situation is normal. Why create unnecessary problems?"
A U.S. embassy spokeswoman said in reaction to the Burmese spokeman's statement: "We won't dignify that comment with our response, other than to firmly reject any such assertions."

This month Burma has been hit by the worst anti-government protests since the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) crushed a democracy uprising in 1988. Student protesters have staged rallies and sit-ins around the capital.
On Friday the protest showed signs of slowing, as SLORC stationed tanks and troop-carrying trucks around Rangoon's city hall area to thwart any fresh demonstrations, witnesses said.
Access to Suu Kyi's lakeside residence on University Avenue has been blocked by the SLORC during the unrest.

The European Union (EU) said on Friday it was deeply concerned by reports of police brutality in dispersing the demonstrations and called on SLORC to enter into meaningful dialogue with pro-democracy groups.

"The EU affirms the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of expression and calls on all sides to show restraint and to prevent any further deterioration in the situation," EU President Ireland said in a statement on behalf of the 15-nation bloc.

The U.N. resolution, passed on Thursday, called on SLORC to free political prisoners and enter into a "substantive political dialogue" with Suu Kyi whose National League for Democracy was suppressed after winning 1990 elections.

Washington's U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright said SLORC did not meet minimum human rights standards, adding it had suppressed non-political protests and imposed the most severe restrictions on Suu Kyi since her 1995 release from house arrest.

"The Burmese authorities would like the world to believe that its harsh policies are necessary in light of Burma's turbulent history. But the world does not accept that excuse," she told the assembly.

Earlier this week, the Burmese government spokesman said that the U.S. embassy had tried to encourage the opposition leader to leave her compound, knowing that if she were stopped, it could be used as an excuse by the United States to impose sanctions.
The U.S. Senate in July passed legislation allowing President Bill Clinton to impose economic sanctions if repressions in Burma worsened or if Suu Kyi were rearrested.
